subtype: Cheek movement in fatigue and stress [Regulating]
passage:
The generator at the printing press had failed at four, and Rafiq had until nine to get two thousand exam booklets bound for the district office. Under the one working tube light, he puffed out a long breath, cheeks ballooning, then clenched his jaw so hard the muscles in his cheeks jumped.
Sabina, feeding covers into the stapler, glanced up. "That's the third time you've done the balloon face."
"What face?"
She puffed her own cheeks to show him. He laughed despite himself, then noticed how tight his face felt, like a fist.
"Five minutes," Sabina said. "Go stand outside. I'll keep stapling."
He stood by the gate in the drizzle, let his jaw hang loose and breathed slowly. When he came back, he spotted the missing box of covers he had walked past twice.

qa.q: How many exam booklets did Rafiq need to get bound?
qa.a: Rafiq had to get two thousand exam booklets bound for the district office.

qa.q: What did Rafiq's puffed cheeks and clenched jaw suggest?
qa.a: They suggested Rafiq was tense and stressed about the nine o'clock deadline; they might also have shown plain tiredness after the power failed.

qa.q: What small step helped Rafiq get back on track?
qa.a: A five-minute break outside, letting his jaw loosen and breathing slowly, cleared his head enough to spot the missing box of covers.

qa.q: How did Sabina see the balloon face?
qa.a: Sabina read it as a sign he was strained, so she mirrored it back lightly and kept stapling so he could step out.

grounding: Puffed cheeks and a clenched jaw signal stress; noticing them leads to a short break, and a colleague offers gentle support.

passage:
"And Jaya will also take the vendor onboarding, since she's so organised."
Jaya pressed her lips into a thin line and wrote it down.
After the meeting, Gargi caught up with her by the lift. "You did the zip-mouth thing again."
"What zip-mouth thing?"
"Lips pressed flat, like you're holding a sentence between your teeth. Third meeting this month."
"Because if I'd opened my mouth, I'd have said, 'I'm already on two launches, are you joking?'"
"Fair. Holding that in the room was probably smart. But you keep swallowing it, and then you're cranky all week."
"So what, I just complain?"
"Not complain. Ask. Book fifteen minutes with our manager tomorrow. Say you want to do the onboarding properly, and ask which launch can slip."
Jaya let out a breath. "Tomorrow. Before I lose my nerve."

qa.q: What extra task was Jaya given in the meeting?
qa.a: Jaya was given the vendor onboarding.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she pressed her lips together?
qa.a: Jaya felt frustrated and overloaded, already on two launches, and was holding back a sharp comment; the pressed lips could also have looked like concentration, which is why Gargi's reading was a guess until Jaya explained.

qa.q: What would you advise Jaya to do about the extra work?
qa.a: Meet the manager calmly the next day, say she wants to do the onboarding properly, and ask which launch can slip.

qa.q: What is it like for Gargi to watch Jaya swallow her words each time?
qa.a: Gargi sees the pattern and the crankiness that follows, so she is concerned and nudges Jaya to speak up in a calm way.

grounding: Pressed lips show restraint in a tense meeting, and calmly raising the concern later is better than swallowing it every time.

subtype: Trembling voice and lips at emotional moments [Regulating]
passage:
Disha, you missed the best part of the farewell. Ramaiah sir, the lab head who took a chance on me, was retiring, and they asked me to speak. When they called out "Harsha from the protein lab," I walked up with it all typed out. Two lines in, I got to "he gave a nervous kid a key to the lab at night," and my lips started shaking. Actually shaking. My voice went thin.
I thought I'd die of embarrassment. Instead I stopped, looked at the page, and breathed out slowly, twice. The whole room just waited. Nobody coughed, nobody laughed. Ramaiah sir took his glasses off.
Then I finished. Slower than planned, but I finished. Afterwards the new intern told me the pause was the part she remembered most. Funny, right? The bit I was most scared of turned out to be the bit that worked.

qa.q: What line was Harsha reading when the lips started shaking?
qa.a: The line was "he gave a nervous kid a key to the lab at night."

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when the lips began to tremble?
qa.a: Harsha was deeply moved by gratitude to Ramaiah sir and, at the same time, embarrassed and scared of breaking down in front of everyone.

qa.q: What helped Harsha get through the speech?
qa.a: Stopping, looking at the page and breathing out slowly twice, then finishing at a slower pace instead of rushing.

qa.q: How did the audience respond to the pause?
qa.a: The room waited patiently without coughing or laughing, and the intern even remembered the pause as the best part.

grounding: Trembling lips while speaking about something moving are a normal sign of strong feeling; a slow breath and a pause help, and listeners wait patiently.

passage:
"You moved my Saturday shift without asking me," Elizabeth said, chin forward, jaw pushed out.
Kashish felt her own shoulders rise. She kept her voice low. "You're upset about the rota. Tell me what happened."
"I found out from the board. Again."
"Okay. That's on me; I should have messaged you. Is it the Saturday itself, or finding out that way?"
Elizabeth's jaw stayed set. "Both. My mother's hospital visit is on Saturday."
"Ah. I didn't know. What time is it?"
"Morning."
"If I swap you to the late shift, does that work?"
A pause. The jaw eased a little. "Yes. That works."
Kashish nodded. Earlier, when Elizabeth's voice had risen, she had kept one eye on the open door and a plan to step out if it got any louder. She hadn't needed it.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth find out her shift had been moved?
qa.a: She found out from the board.

qa.q: What might Elizabeth's jutting jaw suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: Most likely Elizabeth felt angry and determined to be heard about the shift; it could also have been worry about her mother's hospital visit coming out as defensiveness.

qa.q: Which choices helped Kashish calm the exchange?
qa.a: Keeping her voice low, owning the missed message, asking what mattered and offering the late shift, while keeping a way to step out if it turned unsafe.

qa.q: What would have changed if Kashish had matched Elizabeth's tone?
qa.a: The argument would likely have grown louder and Elizabeth might never have mentioned the hospital visit, so no fix would have been found.

grounding: A jutting jaw in a disagreement may mean resolve, defensiveness or fear; staying calm and asking questions de-escalates, with leaving kept as an option.

subtype: Tongue in cheek humour at work [Mismatch]
passage:
The new timetable went up on the office noticeboard in Kochi at ten: four meetings on Friday, one titled "Reducing Meetings." Jomon read it, pushed his tongue into his cheek so it bulged, and said flatly, "Wonderful. Finally, a meeting to reduce meetings. I'll bring snacks."
Two of the old-timers snorted. Charu, who had joined on Monday, went still. She looked from the noticeboard to Jomon and back, then quietly asked, "Should I tell someone you're not happy with it?"
Jomon saw that she had caught the flat voice but not the bulge in his cheek. He grinned properly this time. "No, no. Joke. I'm fine with it, really. I just find the title funny."
Charu let out a breath and smiled. "Okay. I honestly couldn't tell."
"Fair. You don't know my face yet," Jomon said. "I'll smile more till you do."

qa.q: What was the title of one of the Friday meetings?
qa.a: One meeting was titled "Reducing Meetings."

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she asked if she should tell someone?
qa.a: Charu felt unsure and a little worried, reading Jomon's flat voice as a real complaint because she did not yet know his dry humour.

qa.q: What could Jomon keep doing with newer colleagues?
qa.a: Add a clear smile or say it is a joke, since people who don't know him yet may miss the tongue-in-cheek face. 🙂

qa.q: Why did the old-timers react differently from Charu?
qa.a: They knew Jomon's dry style, so they read the bulging cheek as a joke, while Charu had only been there since Monday.

grounding: A tongue-in-cheek face with a dry remark signals a joke to people who know the speaker, but a newcomer can miss it until a smile clarifies.

subtype: Blank expression in exhaustion or burnout [Interpreting]
passage:
Hi Charu,
I wanted to write rather than catch you in the corridor, because this isn't about the quality of your work.
For the past few weeks I've noticed you look very still in our stand-ups, no reaction even when someone told that terrible pun about the printer. I'll admit that at first I wondered if you'd lost interest in the project. Then I remembered you stayed till nine twice last week and never said a word about it.
So I'm not assuming anything. You might be tired, or a lot might be going on, or I might be reading too much into a face. If you're carrying too much, I can move the vendor reports to another teammate for a month, and you can skip Friday's call.
Would you like to grab coffee on Thursday, just us? No agenda.
Take care,
Uma

qa.q: What does Uma offer to move to another teammate?
qa.a: Uma offers to move the vendor reports to another teammate for a month.

qa.q: What was Uma worried about on first noticing Charu's still face?
qa.a: Uma was first worried that Charu had lost interest in the project, but felt less sure after remembering that Charu stayed till nine twice last week.

qa.q: What makes Uma's email a kind check-in?
qa.a: It is private, says it isn't about work quality, avoids assuming, and offers practical help plus an unhurried coffee.

qa.q: How might Charu feel reading the email?
qa.a: Charu might feel relieved and seen, since the email offers help without judging; Charu could also feel a bit exposed that the blank face was noticed.

grounding: A colleague's blank face for weeks may come from exhaustion or overload rather than lack of interest, so a private, kind check-in with practical help is offered.

passage:
In the staffroom of the Nagpur school, Rukmini caught her reflection in the glass of the trophy cupboard and barely recognised it: jaw locked, brows pinched, mouth a hard line. In ten minutes she had to tell Ojas that the science fair plan he had presented as his own was mostly hers.
If she walked in with that face, he'd get defensive before she said a word.
She sat down, put her palms flat on the table, and breathed in for four counts, out for six. She let her shoulders drop away from her ears. She unclenched her back teeth. Again. By the fourth breath her forehead felt looser.
When Ojas came in, she said, "Can we talk about the fair plan? I think some of my part got lost." Her voice came out even. He blinked, then nodded. "Okay. Show me."

qa.q: Where did Rukmini see her reflection?
qa.a: She saw it in the glass of the trophy cupboard.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini want to soften her face before Ojas came in?
qa.a: Rukmini felt tense and angry that her work had been passed off, and she feared a hard face would make Ojas defensive before she even spoke.

qa.q: What steps did Rukmini use to relax her face?
qa.a: She put her palms flat, breathed in for four and out for six, let her shoulders drop and unclenched her back teeth, repeating it until her forehead loosened.

qa.q: What would change if Rukmini had walked in with a locked jaw?
qa.a: Ojas might have felt attacked and turned defensive at once, making a fair talk about the plan much harder.

grounding: Before a hard talk, an adult notices a rigid face and softens it with slow breaths and loose shoulders, which makes the conversation go more easily.

passage:
At the Monday meeting of the community centre, Pradeep laid out his plan: the evening tuition classes would move to seven in the morning. Swati nodded. She nodded when he mentioned the cheaper electricity, nodded when he showed the new timetable, nodded when he said, "So we all agree?"
Then she heard herself thinking: half my Class 8 kids sell vegetables with their parents at seven.
Her head was still bobbing. She stopped it.
"Pradeep, sorry, I've been nodding, but I actually have a worry." Her cheeks went warm. "Many of my students work in the mornings. We might lose them."
Pradeep frowned, then pulled the timetable back towards him. "I didn't know that. Could we try mornings only for the younger batch?"
"That could work. I'll ask the parents this week."

qa.q: What time would the tuition classes move to?
qa.a: The classes would move to seven in the morning.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when she noticed her head still bobbing?
qa.a: Swati felt uneasy and a little embarrassed, because the nodding showed agreement she did not feel while she was worried the plan would lose her students.

qa.q: What went right once Swati spoke up?
qa.a: She admitted the nodding, gave one concrete concern about her students and stayed respectful, which let Pradeep suggest a middle path. 👍

qa.q: How might Pradeep have read Swati's nodding before she spoke?
qa.a: Pradeep probably took it as agreement and support, so he only learned about the working students because she voiced her concern.

grounding: Steady nodding can look like support while hiding disagreement, and voicing the concern respectfully leads to a better plan.

subtype: Bowing the head in respect and mourning [Expressing]
passage:
The community hall behind the factory had been cleared for the prayer meeting for Irawati's father. Nilesh stood at the back, unsure what to do with his hands. He had never been to a Buddhist memorial before.
When the monk began to chant, Irawati, dressed in white, pressed her palms together and bowed her head low. The people around her did the same. Nilesh lowered his head too, eyes on the floor, and stayed that way until the chanting ended.
It struck him later that he had bowed his head that very morning as well: a quick dip with a smile when the retired founder visited the plant, a sign of respect. Here the same movement meant something heavier: sharing grief, keeping quiet.
At the door he joined his palms to Irawati. She bowed back slightly, eyes tired, and whispered, "Thank you for coming."

qa.q: What was Irawati dressed in at the prayer meeting?
qa.a: Irawati was dressed in white.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling as he stood at the back?
qa.a: Nilesh felt unsure and a little awkward, since he did not know the customs of a Buddhist memorial or what to do with his hands.

qa.q: What was wise about how Nilesh handled an unfamiliar ritual?
qa.a: He watched Irawati and the people around her and followed their lead, bowing his head quietly until the chanting ended.

qa.q: What might the bow have meant to Irawati?
qa.a: It likely showed Irawati that he respected her father and shared her grief, which is why she bowed back and thanked him.

grounding: Bowing the head can signal respect at a formal greeting and grief at a memorial, and an observer follows the local custom.
